subject: Feature superposition geometry changes in residual stream representations across fine-tuning regimes in sparse autoencoders

Topic: Feature superposition geometry changes in residual stream representations across fine-tuning regimes in sparse autoencoders

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1966)
response:
The central question is: when you fine-tune a pretrained transformer, does the sparse autoencoder (SAE) you trained on the base model still faithfully decompose the fine-tuned model's residual stream, or has the underlying geometric structure of feature superposition shifted enough that you're now getting a mismatched dictionary? Superposition refers to the phenomenon where models pack more features than dimensions into the residual stream by exploiting near-orthogonality in high-dimensional space — the geometry (angles, norms, interference patterns between feature directions) encodes which features are co-active and how strongly. Fine-tuning doesn't just adjust which features fire; it can rotate, rescale, or merge feature directions, split previously superposed concepts, or introduce entirely new superposition configurations tuned to the target domain. An expert worries about basis drift — the SAE's learned dictionary vectors becoming misaligned with the post-fine-tuning feature directions — meaning reconstruction error rises selectively on the new task's activations while appearing acceptable on average, masking the failure. The subtler concern is that fine-tuning under different data regimes (RLHF, instruction tuning, domain adaptation) likely imposes systematically different superposition geometries reflecting different feature co-occurrence statistics, so a single SAE topology may not be flexible enough to capture both regimes, and naive transfer produces ghost features (SAE neurons that activate but correspond to no coherent semantic direction in the fine-tuned model).

NEXT: If you retrain an SAE from scratch on the fine-tuned model and compare its dictionary to the base model's SAE dictionary, what geometric relationship would you expect between the two learned bases, and how would you actually measure whether a feature has been "preserved," "rotated," or "destroyed"?

If you retrain an SAE from scratch on the fine-tuned model and compare its dictionary to the base model's SAE dictionary, what geometric relationship would you expect between the two learned bases, and how would you actually measure whether a feature has been "preserved," "rotated," or "destroyed"?

The two learned bases will not be in arbitrary relative position — you'd expect a large stable core of features that align well across the two SAEs (high cosine similarity between matched dictionary vectors), a smaller set of rotated features where the direction has shifted but the concept is recoverable, and a tail of destroyed or emergent features with no good match. Anthropic's work on SAE features across layers (e.g., in their April 2024 "Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders" paper) shows that even within a single model, SAE dictionaries at nearby layers share substantial structure, which gives a baseline expectation that moderate fine-tuning preserves most geometry. To measure preservation concretely, you'd compute a bipartite matching between the two dictionaries using cosine similarity — specifically something like the Hungarian algorithm or a greedy nearest-neighbor match — and look at the distribution of matched cosine similarities; a peak near 1.0 indicates preserved features, a flat or bimodal distribution signals structural reorganization. "Rotation" specifically means a matched pair has high cosine similarity (say >0.7) but the feature's activation frequency and co-activation neighborhood has changed, indicating the direction survived but its functional role shifted — you'd catch this by comparing the top activating examples across models for the matched pair. "Destruction" is operationalized as a feature's best match falling below some threshold (Marks et al. and the Neuronpedia tooling implicitly use ~0.5 as a soft cutoff) combined with the base-model feature's activation rate dropping near zero in the fine-tuned model's distribution. The expert worry here is that the matching procedure itself is ill-posed when fine-tuning induces feature splitting or merging — one base feature becomes two fine-tuned features, or two merge into one — because bipartite matching assumes a one-to-one correspondence that the geometry may have genuinely broken.

prompt:
When fine-tuning induces feature splitting — one base SAE feature becoming two or more finer-grained fine-tuned SAE features — what does that imply about the sparsity coefficient (L1 penalty) you should use when training the fine-tuned SAE, and how would you detect that your L1 is set wrong for the new regime?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1968)
response:
Feature splitting implies the fine-tuned model is using more features per residual stream position to represent concepts that were previously conflated — the effective sparsity of the underlying representation has decreased locally in the fine-tuned domain, meaning you need a lower L1 coefficient to allow the SAE to use those additional dictionary vectors without penalizing them into silence. If you keep the base model's L1 setting, the penalty will suppress the newly differentiated features back into a single merged activation, recreating the pre-split geometry artificially and giving you a falsely clean dictionary that hides the actual increased representational granularity. Anthropic's "Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders" (Gao et al., 2024) demonstrates that L1 coefficient directly controls the L0 (average number of active features per token) in a roughly linear-log relationship, and they note that reconstruction fidelity on held-out data degrades sharply when L0 is too low for a given model scale — the same logic applies when the fine-tuned domain structurally demands higher L0. The concrete detection signal for a miscalibrated L1 is a bimodal reconstruction error distribution: tokens from the fine-tuned domain will show systematically higher MSE or cross-entropy loss recovered than base-domain tokens, even after matching for token frequency, because the SAE can't allocate enough simultaneous features to represent the richer decomposition. A subtler signal is feature absorption, described by Bricken et al. and more explicitly in Marks et al. (2024) — where one over-burdened feature shows anomalously high activation frequency and broad, semantically incoherent top-activating examples, which is the dictionary's symptom of being forced to represent multiple concepts with a single vector due to excessive L1 pressure. The right calibration procedure is to sweep L1 while monitoring both L0 on fine-tuned-domain data specifically and the kurtosis of the activation distribution per dictionary vector — correctly split features will show sharper, more kurtotic activations than merged ones, so a properly tuned fine-tuned SAE should have higher mean kurtosis across its dictionary than the base SAE.

The sharpest criterion is causal interventional consistency: a genuine split produces two features where activating each one independently via steering or clamping causes the model to behave differently in semantically coherent, distinguishable ways, whereas a false split produces two features that cause nearly identical downstream behavioral changes when intervened on separately. This is operationalizable using activation patching — if feature A and feature B are candidate split products, patch each into a clean prompt and measure the KL divergence between the resulting output distributions; genuine splits should show high inter-feature KL (they do different things) while false splits cluster near zero. A second criterion is conditional co-activation exclusivity: genuine split features should be mutually suppressive — when one fires strongly, the other should fire weakly or not at all on the same token — because they represent differentiated sub-concepts that don't co-occur; false splits from noise will show positive or near-zero correlation in their activation patterns because they're both responding to the same underlying polysemantic signal. Anthropic's interpretability work on superposition (Elhage et al., 2022) predicts that genuine features occupy distinct privileged directions in the residual stream with characteristic interference patterns, so a geometric criterion is also available: genuine split features should have lower mutual cosine similarity (ideally below 0.3) and their activation-weighted covariance in the residual stream should be near-diagonal, while false splits will remain highly correlated in activation space even if their dictionary vectors look distinct. The hardest case — which experts worry about and beginners miss entirely — is context-dependent splits, where a feature genuinely differentiates in some fine-tuned contexts but collapses back to a single representation in others, meaning the split is real but conditional; here you need to stratify your co-activation and intervention tests by context type rather than averaging across the full distribution, or you'll classify genuine conditional splits as false positives.

Since causal intervention tests require steering or patching individual SAE features, and fine-tuning may have shifted the residual stream geometry such that the SAE's encoder and decoder directions are no longer aligned (i.e., the SAE has non-negligible encoder-decoder asymmetry post fine-tuning), how does that asymmetry corrupt your intervention results, and what should you do about it?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1970)
response:
Encoder-decoder asymmetry means the direction the SAE uses to detect a feature (encoder weight) diverges from the direction it uses to write that feature back into the residual stream (decoder weight), and this corrupts interventions because when you clamp or patch via the decoder direction, you're injecting a vector that the encoder may not recognize as that feature — and worse, that the model's downstream attention and MLP layers were not trained to respond to in the way you intend. Concretely, if you add λ·d_i (the i-th decoder column) to the residual stream to "activate feature i," but the true causal direction for that concept in the fine-tuned model has rotated 40° away from d_i, you're injecting a mixture of the intended feature and whatever other features project onto that decoder direction — your intervention result is a superposition of multiple causal signals, and any behavioral change you measure is uninterpretable as evidence about feature i specifically. This problem is known in the SAE literature as the feature geometry inconsistency problem and is related to the "shrinkage" issue documented by Sharkey et al. and discussed in Anthropic's April 2024 SAE paper — the L1 penalty systematically biases decoder norms downward and encoder directions toward high-variance data directions, creating asymmetry even in the base model, which fine-tuning then exacerbates. To detect the asymmetry magnitude, compute cosine similarity between each encoder row e_i and its corresponding decoder column d_i across the dictionary — in a well-trained base SAE these typically hover around 0.85–0.95, but post fine-tuning on a shifted distribution you should expect a population of features dropping below 0.7, with the worst offenders being exactly the features that underwent splitting or rotation. The practical fix used in recent work (e.g., the "end-to-end SAE" approach from Braun et al., 2024) is to train with a reconstruction-in-model-behavior objective rather than pure L2+L1 on activations, which forces encoder and decoder to stay causally consistent because the loss propagates through the model's forward pass — but this is expensive, so a cheaper approximation is to re-normalize decoder columns to unit length and fine-tune only the encoder on the new distribution while freezing the decoder, reducing asymmetry growth without full retraining. The intervention result you should trust most under residual asymmetry is not the absolute behavioral change from a single feature patch, but the differential between patching d_i versus patching a random direction with the same norm — genuine features will show anomalously large differential effects even under asymmetry, because the decoder direction still carries signal even if it's noisy.

response:
The assumption breaks most severely under three conditions: heavy RLHF or preference optimization that introduces new reward-relevant feature directions with no base model analog (e.g., a "sycophancy" or "refusal" direction that emerges de novo), domain adaptation to a highly specialized vocabulary where the residual stream develops new high-variance directions orthogonal to the base model's principal components, and catastrophic forgetting regimes where the fine-tuning loss actively suppresses base model features to free up representational capacity — in all three cases, the true fine-tuned feature directions live in subspaces that the frozen decoder simply doesn't span. A concrete quantitative threshold: if the fine-tuned model's residual stream activations, when projected onto the frozen decoder's column space, leave more than ~15-20% of variance unexplained (measurable via PCA on the reconstruction residual), the decoder is missing directions that matter and frozen-decoder encoder fine-tuning will systematically fail to capture those features regardless of how well you retrain the encoder. The detection procedure before committing to the repair is to run a probe sweep: train linear probes on the fine-tuned model's residual stream for behaviors or concepts that are new to the fine-tuned domain (e.g., instruction-following compliance, domain-specific entity types), then check whether those probe directions have high cosine similarity with any frozen decoder column — if the best match is below ~0.4, the decoder doesn't contain the needed direction and freezing it will blind the SAE to that concept entirely. A subtler signal is the dead feature rate after encoder-only fine-tuning: if a large fraction of decoder columns (say >20%) have near-zero activation frequency on fine-tuned-domain data even after encoder retraining, those decoder directions are irrelevant to the new geometry and the SAE has effectively lost that capacity — compare this to the dead feature rate from a fully retrained SAE on the same data to quantify the gap. The hardest violation to detect in advance is basis rotation without subspace expansion — where the fine-tuning rotates existing feature directions substantially but doesn't add new ones, meaning the decoder still spans the right subspace but individual columns point in wrong directions — because the variance-explained diagnostic will look acceptable while individual feature reconstructions are badly misaligned; catching this requires checking per-feature reconstruction fidelity on fine-tuned activations, not just aggregate R².

Yes, and there's concrete evidence this is already happening: mechanistic interpretability work on fine-tuned models (e.g., Jain et al. on RLHF, and the "Refusal in LLMs" work by Arditi et al. 2024) finds that fine-tuning often concentrates behavioral changes in specific layers rather than distributing them uniformly, meaning a per-layer SAE at the "wrong" layer will see almost none of the fine-tuning signal while one at the "right" layer sees a massive geometric disruption — the per-layer framing doesn't fail uniformly, it fails selectively in ways that are invisible unless you're monitoring all layers simultaneously. The deeper structural problem is that the residual stream is a running sum, and a feature that in the base model was written at layer 8 and read at layer 12 may, after fine-tuning, be written at layer 6 and read at layer 10 — the feature still exists and functions causally, but a per-layer SAE at layer 8 will report it as destroyed while the layer 6 SAE reports it as emergent, giving a completely misleading picture of what fine-tuning actually did. This motivates cross-layer or trajectory-based decomposition approaches, where you treat the full residual stream trajectory (the sequence of layer-wise vectors) as the object to decompose rather than any single slice — work like Lindsey et al.'s "cross-coders" (Anthropic, 2024) explicitly trains SAEs that span multiple layers and finds features with characteristic multi-layer activation signatures that are invisible to per-layer analysis. The right unit of analysis for fine-tuned models is arguably the computational pathway — the (layer, head/MLP, feature) triple that implements a specific transformation — and fine-tuning audits should track whether pathways are rerouted, short-circuited, or newly created, not just whether individual layer-wise dictionaries change. The practical difficulty is that cross-layer SAEs have a combinatorially larger input space and require far more data and compute to train well, which is why the field has defaulted to per-layer analysis despite its known limitations — but for fine-tuning comparisons specifically, a cheaper proxy is to compute layer-wise residual stream similarity (CKA or representational similarity analysis) between base and fine-tuned models across all layers simultaneously, which at least localizes where the geometric disruption is concentrated before committing to where to place your SAEs.

The causal direction is most likely neither cleanly cause nor consequence but rather a co-adapted pair: gradient descent during fine-tuning simultaneously adjusts MLP write directions and attention read directions in a coordinated way because the loss propagates through both, meaning what you observe as "layer redistribution" is actually the visible signature of a joint optimization that doesn't respect the cause/effect framing — this is why activation patching experiments on fine-tuned models often find that patching either the MLP output or the attention pattern alone only partially recovers or disrupts a behavior, with full effect requiring both. The most concrete evidence for co-adaptation comes from the circuit-level fine-tuning analysis in work like Prakash et al. (2024) on how RLHF affects circuits, which finds that fine-tuning modifies attention head weights and MLP weights in correlated ways within the same circuit, suggesting the optimizer is moving them together rather than one dragging the other. However, the causal direction does matter practically for reversal interventions: if attention pattern shift is upstream (the head learned to route tokens to a new layer where an MLP then writes the feature), then intervening on the attention head is the minimal and most generalizable fix — you restore the routing and the downstream MLP behavior follows without modification; whereas if the MLP write-layer shift is upstream (an MLP at a new layer started writing a feature, and attention heads then adapted to read it there), patching the attention pattern alone will fail because the feature is no longer being written at the old location. A concrete diagnostic to determine which is upstream is freezing one component type and fine-tuning only the other: if freezing all attention weights during fine-tuning still produces the layer redistribution (MLPs shift their write layers alone), then MLP changes are upstream; if freezing MLPs prevents redistribution, attention is upstream — this is a tractable ablation that hasn't been done systematically in published work but is directly implied by the LoRA fine-tuning literature, where applying LoRA only to attention weights versus only to MLP weights produces qualitatively different behavioral profiles. The reason this matters acutely for reversal is that minimal interventions generalize better: if you want to undo a fine-tuning effect (e.g., remove a sycophancy behavior introduced by RLHF) by editing model weights or steering activations, intervening at the true upstream cause will affect only the targeted behavior, while intervening downstream will require compensating for all the co-adaptations that followed, risking collateral damage to unrelated capabilities — this is precisely the failure mode observed in blunt refusal-direction ablations that degrade general capability alongside the targeted behavior.
